items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I’d worked with James P. Johnson. I was tight with him. James P. Johnson . . . At that time I was working with James P. Johnson before I joined Benny Carter.

ctx.x: Me and him were tight. I’d worked with James P. Johnson. I was tight with him. James P. Johnson . . . At that time I was working with James P. Johnson before I joined Benny Carter. Between Cab. James P. Johnson heard the record, Don’t You Feel My Legs, say, “You got a hit. I’m working with you.” He said . . . I said, “Yeah.” He said, “Yeah, but bring your vasoline.” I said, “Bring my vasoline for what?” He said, “Because you’re going to get screwed.” [? (inaudible)] know what that mean. He wrote The Charleston,…

keys—they do that, piano players, when they’re playing—raise my hand. Don’t touch a note. Then come right in. He said, “I never seen nobody do that. That’s what you call respect.” And I gets that from “The Lion” in front of a gang of people. Not a gang of people. About six critical musicians.

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: I'd go to James P. Johnson's house, and they all were welcome in his house.

ctx.x: He was kind of tall, and he smiled all the time. But he had a strange name. He would be in there. And James P. Johnson would come through there. Fats Waller come through there.

Jelly Roll stood on the corner. They didn't understand Jelly Roll. Jelly Roll would be talkin' like he talked to night people, who understand Jelly Roll... Jelly Roll would stand out in front of the club and talk to all these defeated musicians; half of them couldn't play, including me. We'd stand around there waiting for a gig and looking up at Jelly Roll. Well, Jelly Roll is from home. But Jelly Roll, he loves an audience. I noticed Jelly Roll had two little things on the end of his jaw that he could establish…
